red.focus: Find evidence without assuming the client’s account is complete.
red.summary: Lawful factfinding can confirm, qualify, or contradict a claim. Learn why discovery serves truth, while relevance, privacy, and procedural rules limit what may be demanded.
checklist: I can identify the evidence needed to test a factual claim
I can distinguish relevance from unrestricted access
I can explain the importance of preserving records

sections.title: Start with a question, not a pile of documents
sections.body_md: An employee says their employer sent a dismissal notice on the wrong date. The lawyer needs the notice, transmission records, and relevant testimony. Discovery is a regulated process for obtaining or exchanging evidence in systems that use it. Other jurisdictions structure factfinding differently. In every system, the aim is to test the legal questions that matter. A demand for every document about the employer is less useful than a careful inquiry into the date and authority of the actual decision.

sections.title: Relevant does not mean unlimited
sections.body_md: Evidence is relevant when it can help resolve an issue the law treats as material. Yet relevant material may still be protected by privacy, legal privilege, confidentiality rules, or proportionality. A lawsuit is not permission to search every opponent’s private communication. Before requesting information, ask which proposition it could prove or disprove and whether the forum permits obtaining it. This protects the accuracy of the case and the dignity of persons who may never become parties.

sections.title: A fact can disappear
sections.body_md: Electronic messages may be deleted routinely, and witnesses' memories can fade. Preservation duties may arise when litigation is reasonably anticipated under applicable law, but the exact timing and obligations vary. The lawyer should identify likely evidence, explain lawful preservation, and record any gaps honestly. Inventing a missing email or altering a screenshot is never a substitute for proof. A reliable process gives both sides the best available opportunity to establish what actually happened.

yellow.summary: Document requests, interrogatories, depositions, and admissions serve different purposes. Learn how counsel chooses a proportionate method while respecting privilege.
checklist: I can distinguish major fact-gathering tools
I can identify the limits of legal privilege
I can evaluate whether a request is proportionate

sections.title: Choose the evidence method
sections.body_md: A document request seeks existing records; an interrogatory asks an opposing party a written question under applicable procedures; a deposition records sworn testimony in systems that permit it. A request for admission narrows disputed propositions. These tools are not universally available in the same forms. A good lawyer knows what question the evidence must answer before choosing a method. More questions and documents can create expense without improving the accuracy of a decision.

sections.title: Privilege is a legal rule, not a label
sections.body_md: A client may disclose sensitive facts to legal counsel for advice. Attorney–client privilege and work-product protections can restrict disclosure under specified rules, but their holders, scope, and exceptions vary by legal system. Marking an email confidential does not necessarily make it privileged; equally, the facts underlying a protected communication may still be discoverable elsewhere. An advocate must examine the rule, purpose, and potential waiver before assuring a client that a record can never be disclosed.

sections.title: Proportionality governs scope
sections.body_md: A request covering ten years of files may be relevant to a limited degree but impose excessive costs compared with the matter in dispute. Courts may narrow requests or protect sensitive information. A proposed response should identify the factual issue, the necessary time period, available alternatives, and the burden of collection. The goal is enough reliable evidence to permit a fair decision, not maximum disclosure. Proportionality can serve the claimant and the opponent together.

orange.focus: Design reliable factfinding under informational inequality.
orange.summary: Large institutions may control the records required to challenge their conduct. Develop evidence requests that target factual hypotheses, preserve authenticity, and protect nonparties.
checklist: I can identify how information asymmetry affects proof

sections.title: Start with a falsifiable hypothesis
sections.body_md: A platform denies a user access after automated screening. A claimant may need decision logs, relevant criteria, and the account history rather than the platform's entire database. Ask what evidence would confirm or challenge each claimed legal element. A staged request can reduce costs and protect third-party privacy while bringing critical records into view. The difficulty is not merely retrieving data; it is choosing an inquiry that a tribunal can interpret and test.

sections.title: Records need a trustworthy history
sections.body_md: A screenshot may omit context; an exported log may have lost timestamps or been modified by processing. Authentication and chain-of-custody records help establish whether a document is what its proponent claims. Identify collection methods, custody, metadata, and any transformation. Technical evidence should be explained in terms a factfinder can evaluate. It is a mistake to treat more data as stronger evidence automatically: quantity cannot replace demonstrated reliability.

sections.title: Balance access and protected interests
sections.body_md: An employer's internal messages might reveal discrimination while also containing private health information about unrelated employees. A court may authorize redaction, confidentiality restrictions, or in-camera review where applicable rules permit. An advanced proposal explains why particular records are material and why the chosen protective measure permits meaningful challenge. The parties' incentives should be examined rather than assumed: concealment and overdisclosure can both harm justice. The client deserves evidence that is usable, not merely voluminous.

black.focus: Evaluate discovery as a distribution of institutional power.
black.summary: Evidence rules decide who can expose a wrong and who must bear the cost of investigation. Defend a factfinding system that protects truth, privacy, and equal access.
checklist: I can assess the costs of disclosure and secrecy
I can recognize litigation expense as potential leverage
I can propose reviewable and proportionate evidence procedures

sections.title: Disclosure makes power visible
sections.body_md: An institution may possess all records of a harmful decision, while the person affected has only its consequences. A generous disclosure rule can reveal misconduct, yet broad demands can expose intimate data or bankrupt a small opponent. Discovery therefore allocates power before a final merits judgment. A doctoral analysis identifies who controls evidence, the cost of producing it, and the harms of both exclusion and excessive disclosure. There is no morally neutral choice to request everything or nothing.

sections.title: Protected relationships have value
sections.body_md: Legal advice may depend on candid communication, and personal information may deserve protection even when litigation is public. Privilege and confidentiality can serve legitimate ends. But secrecy may also conceal unlawful conduct or deny the vulnerable a meaningful remedy. A principled account distinguishes what existing law protects from reform arguments about what it should protect. It asks whose autonomy, safety, or ability to defend a claim is advanced by the rule, and at whose expense.

sections.title: Design bounded evidence access
sections.body_md: Consider phased disclosure tied to specific legal elements, independent review of contested privilege, redaction of nonparty information, and sanctions for intentional destruction. Evaluate whether the design enables poor claimants to access essential evidence without imposing costs that force smaller defendants to capitulate. Require written reasons for restrictive orders and an appropriate path to challenge them. The objective is accountable truth seeking that treats parties and witnesses as persons rather than raw sources of information.
